h1: A verification layer for papers under submission
h2: A verdict is a pure function of its inputs
On the roadmap, and not built yet
h3: Bolded value is best in its block
Every finding has a contest action one click away.
Does a language model decide any of this?
Why does so much come back unverifiable?
Where do the numbers come from?
h4: Reasons a check declines to answer

The same paper checked twice gives the same answer. A language model never produces a verdict. Models extract structure, and every verdict is computed by deterministic Python from that structure. A check that cannot be made deterministic returns unverifiable with a stated reason rather than a guess. A run where much of the paper comes back unverifiable is a success, not a shortfall.

None of this runs yet. It is listed because it is the direction, not because you can use it. Everything above this section works today on the corpus in this repository, and nothing on the roadmap is counted in those numbers.
Feel free to contact me if having any questions. I'm available for new projects or just for chatting.
p: Built for conference and workshop submissions

residual checks whether the numbers a paper states agree with each other. An author runs it before submitting and attaches the report. A reviewer or chair reads it instead of redoing the arithmetic by hand.
It has no opinion on whether a paper is novel, interesting, or correct in its ideas.

A paper states numbers in its abstract, its body text and its tables. residual reads the LaTeX source, recomputes what can be recomputed, and reports where the paper disagrees with itself. The result is a permalink an author can attach to a submission and a reviewer can open.
Find the paper and fetch its source.
Resolve the multi-file LaTeX and build the macro table.
Turn every table cell, link and citation into a checkable claim.
Recompute each claim without deciding anything.
Apply the tolerance policy and assign a verdict.
Each bolded number is compared only against the other numbers in its own rule-delimited block, and only when the column's direction is known.
A column labelled average, mean or overall is recomputed from the other numbers in the same row, to the precision they were printed at.
Every URL printed in the paper is requested, and the ones that no longer resolve are listed.
Every reference in the bibliography is looked up by identifier, never by title containment.
More than one bolded value in a block, so there is no single best.
No arrow in the header and no entry in the direction table.
The value sits in a multicolumn and belongs to no single column.
More than one plausible reading of the row reproduces the stated value.
Contested findings are recorded and rechecked.

Two people. An author, before submitting, who wants the numbers in the paper checked and a report to attach. A reviewer or area chair, who would otherwise redo the arithmetic in a table by hand, or skip it. It verifies numbers, not content, so it does not replace review. It takes one mechanical part off it.

Every finding carries a contest action one click away. Contested findings are recorded and rechecked, and the recheck is deterministic, so a corrected input produces a corrected verdict. Contesting a finding does not suppress it: if it did, contesting would become the way to bury a true finding. Any high-severity diverges finding is held for human review before it appears publicly.

No. A language model never produces a verdict. Models extract structure only, such as which cells are in a table and which claim refers to which cell. Every verdict is computed by deterministic Python from that structure. The four checks in the first release call no model at all.
No. It says nothing about how a paper was written. It reads the numbers the paper states and recomputes them.

Because saying nothing beats saying something wrong about a named researcher’s work. When a table cannot be read without discarding something a verdict might rest on, the check returns unverifiable with a stated reason and attaches the comparison as evidence, so you still see the numbers. A run that declines to answer often is working as intended.

Four things. That each bolded value is the best in its rule-delimited block. That a column labelled average matches the mean of its row. That the URLs printed in the paper still resolve. That every reference in the bibliography exists. Anything beyond those four is on the roadmap and is not running.

The LaTeX source, not the PDF. A paper is often many files joined by input and include, with macros defined in one file and used in another, so the source is resolved and the macro table built before anything is parsed.
An author submits a container image and the run reproduces the numbers in the tables, rather than only recomputing them from the source.
A signed report identifier and an endpoint a chair can call, so a venue can confirm a report belongs to the paper in front of it.
Matching a number stated in the abstract or the body text to the table cell it refers to, and checking that reported variance is consistent.
Checking a baseline number against the paper it was taken from, and scanning a submission for text written to steer a model that reads it.
